evidence.locator: PDF p.2; Section 2.1, Overall Agentic Architecture
evidence.quote: The core iterative cycle (Alg. 1, lines 7-20) involves forecasting, evaluating the forecast against recent ground truth (e.g., via a metric like MAE), and refining the prompt. The Refiner agent can signal early termination if the forecast improve- ment falls below a defined threshold, τstop (e.g., a 5% reduction in MAE). Otherwise, if maximum iterations (Niter) are reached, the system defaults to the prompt that yielded the best observed MAE.

modules.name: Lifecycle roles and communication protocols
modules.scope_reason: Agent roles, workflow memory, review and stop protocols organize execution independently of a temporal output type.

evidence.locator: PDF p.4; Section 3.2, Overview
evidence.quote: Aion ∞is built from six component groups: agents, skills, rules, memory, evaluation, and protocols. Agents are the front-end roles that drive interpretation, evidence collection, solution construction, and review. Skills provide reusable priors and structured workflows that stabilize execution across the lifecycle. Rules define the admissible boundary of the workflow. Memory records progress, decisions, and structural state so that long executions do not drift. Evaluation turns runs into explicit assessment through suites, graders, and final acceptance checks.

evidence.locator: PDF p.4; Section 3.1, Validation interface, Eq. (3)
evidence.quote: Validation interface. V maps a candidate output o to (g, s) = V(o), (3) where g records validity checks such as timestamp alignment, leakage boundaries, or format compliance, and s records scored metrics such as forecasting error, profit, or report quality. modules.name: Temporal task and data interface
modules.scope_reason: Observation units, allowed history, timestamp granularity and data interfaces specify temporal inputs across output forms.

evidence.locator: PDF p.5; Section 3.3.1, Temporal Grounding
evidence.quote: Temporal grounding concerns the parts that are closest to the time series itself. Before asking which model to use, the harness must first determine what counts as one temporal observation, which horizon is requested, and whether the visible data can support that request. In this paper, temporal constraints are the time-related requirements that any valid answer must satisfy, including the observation unit, allowed history and cutoff, forecast or reasoning horizon, timestamp granularity, output frequency, and leakage boundary.

modules.name: Runtime-native temporal objects and tools
modules.scope_reason: Tools operate directly on full-precision temporal objects and return structured observations.

evidence.locator: PDF p.4; Section 3.2, Runtime-Native Temporal Tools
evidence.quote: Unlike conventional tool- augmented agents that must pass data through lan- guage messages, TIMECLAW executes these oper- ations inside the harness runtime, where the full time-series object already resides in the workspace W. Thus, the agent only specifies the intended operation and its parameters without the need to spend context budget on tool interaction. Each tool runs directly on W at numerical precision and returns a compact structured observation.

modules.name: Signal-text episodic retrieval
modules.scope_reason: Retrieval keys jointly represent temporal signal structure and text context, beyond an ordinary dialogue buffer.

evidence.locator: PDF p.4; Section 3.4, Episodic Multimodal Memory
evidence.quote: Episodic memory is common in agentic systems, but its design is nontrivial in contextualized time- series settings, since relevance depends on both task framing and temporal structure. A text-based or jointly serialized retrieval space can (1) re- trieve misleading precedents, since token similarity does not necessarily preserve numerical proximity (Proposition 1); (2) risk modality imbalance for long series; (3) exhibit scale instability, as normal- ization choices can change which temporal patterns appear similar.

modules.name: Fast-slow-reflect forecast revision
modules.scope_reason: The state and actions are defined around a numerical forecast prior and context-conditioned revision.

evidence.locator: PDF p.2; Introduction, framework overview
evidence.quote: In fast-thinking forecasting, CastFSR pro- files historical observations and autonomously selects suit- able lightweight forecasters to construct a data-driven fore- cast prior. In slow deliberative reasoning, it retrieves future- relevant evidence from long-range contextual histories, adap- tively identifies context-specific look-back windows, and rea- sons about how contextual factors reshape future dynamics to refine the forecast prior. In reflective evaluation, CastFSR it- eratively evaluates and adjusts candidate forecasts to enforce temporal regularities, contextual consistency, and domain constraints.

modules.name: Distilled SFT and multi-turn policy training
modules.scope_reason: Supervised distillation and multi-turn RL update the model policy, separately from the forecasting workflow.

evidence.locator: PDF p.4; Model-Agnostic Instantiation of CastFSR, training paragraph
evidence.quote: Specifically, we internalize the workflow in a small model through two-stage training. First, SFT learns executable Fast–Slow–Reflect be- havior from general LLM trajectories distilled on the full cross-domain training data. The validation removes trajecto- ries with illegal tool calls, incorrect stage order, ground-truth leakage, invalid timestamps, or incomplete forecasts. Second, multi-turn RL optimizes complete decision trajectories un- der delayed forecasting feedback.

modules.name: Historical context, scenario and anchor guidance
modules.scope_reason: The output is a future-horizon trajectory conditioned by historical summaries and scenario anchors; generation here is probabilistic prediction.

evidence.locator: PDF p.3; Section IV.A, Framework Overview
evidence.quote: SCENARIODIFF organizes contextual reasoning into three hi- erarchical levels. First, a frozen Historical Context Agent maps M1:L to stepwise context summaries sctx 1:L, grounding the model in document-aligned historical evidence. Second, a frozen Scenario Agent maps (x1:L, sctx 1:L) to a scenario description sscn, projecting a coarse qualitative prior over the forecast horizon. Third, an Anchor Guidance Agent maps (x1:L, sctx 1:L, sscn) to sparse anchor points A, which provide localized constraints for inference-time trajectory refinement.

modules.name: Scenario-conditioned diffusion forecasting
modules.scope_reason: The denoising target is the clean future horizon, not an independent training-data augmentation output.

evidence.locator: PDF p.3; Section IV.A, Framework Overview
evidence.quote: During denoising, the model receives the observed history x1:L, the noisy future x(t), and the contextual conditions produced by the Historical Context Agent and the Scenario Agent. Starting from Gaussian noise, the reverse process generates a trajectory consistent with both numerical history and scenario-level context. Anchor points A are then used by Anchor Blended Sampling to locally refine the generated trajectory.

modules.name: Training-job scheduling and recovery
modules.scope_reason: Queue scheduling, process monitoring and interruption recovery are reusable execution mechanisms, separate from the forecasting objective.

evidence.locator: PDF p.5; Section 3.5, FTAgent execution paragraph
evidence.quote: As shown in Fig. 2, FTAGENT composes pro- grams to train each forecaster with a grid search of hyperparameters. It organizes training jobs – i.e., (forecaster, hyperparameter, dataset) triplets – into a queue and assigns available GPUs for maximally parallel execution. During training, it monitors pro- cesses, resolves errors when encountered, and re- covers interrupted jobs without human intervention. This procedure ends when the queue is emptied.

modules.name: Retrieval, augmentation selection and view review
modules.scope_reason: The reviewed output is a positive view for contrastive representation learning; downstream task evaluation is a separate step.

evidence.locator: PDF p.3; Figure 2 caption
evidence.quote: Our retrieval agent first selects neighborhood candidates with similarity, followed by refinement using an LLM. Our augmentation agent then selects suitable data augmentation strategies from the augmentation strategy library. Finally, our review agent evaluates the quality of the augmented sequences, which approves positive samples into a memory bank and returns to the retrieval agent for refinement if rejected. The augmented views and neighboring samples are utilized as positives for time series representation learning.
